summary: F1's five copies are corrected and now true against BinStore, F3/F5/F6 verified, no cost defect, no pre-emption of M4.3/M4.7/M4.8. But F1 has a SIXTH copy that was not found: Sequencer.java:33-34, inside the 'what a caller may assume' section, still states an affirmative at-most-once application guarantee for flushSeq, contradicting the corrected failure-and-retry paragraph four lines below it. Measured independently: full suite 432 tests, 0 failures, sequencer 17; GATE_SCOPE=full check-module.sh ok, 8 modules.

findings.summary: A SIXTH copy of the retracted at-most-once claim survives, in the contract section itself. Under the heading 'What a caller may NOT assume', the sentence reads: 'Nor that {@code flushSeq} values are seen in order; only that each is applied at most once.' The natural parse of 'nor that X; only that Y' is 'X is not guaranteed; Y is', so this affirmatively promises that a given (podId, flushSeq) is applied at most once. That is exactly the guarantee the F1 fix retracted four lines below ('until it lands a retry after an ambiguous failure may assign a second set of offsets to the same records'), the guarantee FakeSequencer.java:24-27 says it does not model ('a replayed (podId, flushSeq) is treated as a NEW commit and assigned fresh offsets, here and in the real implementation alike'), and the deliverable of M4.10 ('Without this a retried pod is assigned offsets twice'). The fix corrected the failure-and-retry note, the @throws tag, the fake's javadoc, the test's assertion description and the backlog row, and missed the one copy that sits in the section a caller reads to learn what it may rely on. This is the recurring failure mode the M4.0 row itself names: fixing one copy of a fact and missing its duplicates.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.2's implementor, or an author of a retry decorator, or an M4.12 simulation seed reads Sequencer's contract section top-down. Lines 28-34 are the definitive statement of what may and may not be relied on; the reader learns that flushSeq ordering is not guaranteed but that each flushSeq is applied at most once, concludes that duplicate suppression exists, and wraps commit() in a retry on IOException. The store was reachable enough for the conditional PUT to land but the response was lost, the retry assigns a second set of offsets to the same records, and the same documents appear twice in the stream at two different offsets -- the precise silent duplication M4.10 exists to prevent. The contradicting paragraph three paragraphs later does not help a reader who took the contract section at its word, and a contract that states both is not a contract.
findings.suggested_fix: Delete the clause or invert it, e.g. '...Nor that a flushSeq is applied at most once: until M4.10 a replay is assigned fresh offsets -- see the failure-and-retry note below.' No code change; the interface and the fake are already correct.

findings.summary: F2's wrong reason was corrected in the production javadoc but left standing in the test. CommitRequest.java:24-28 now says correctly that the restriction is INHERITED (same identity as SegmentPublisher's podShortId) and that no sequencer key contains podId since M4.0 settled ctl/log/<slot>/... The test comment for aPodIdContainingADashOrSlashIsRefused still gives the old, intrinsic reason verbatim: 'these characters are separators in the key grammar, so a podId carrying one makes a key that parses back to something else.' No key this seam produces embeds podId, so that sentence is false about this class. Verified against SegmentKey.java:71-79, where the reason is genuine (a hyphenated podShortId can spuriously match HEADER_LEN_MARKER in the segment key tail).
findings.failure_scenario: M4.8 or M4.3 needs a key grammar for a per-pod object -- lastAppliedFlushSeq per pod is literally M4.10's data. Someone greps for why podId refuses '-', finds this test comment, believes a sequencer key parses on podId, and either designs the key around a non-existent constraint or, worse, concludes the constraint can be dropped once they confirm no sequencer key contains podId -- which would silently break SegmentPublisher's podShortId identity, the actual reason it exists.

findings.summary: F3 is fixed for the per-entry validation but not for the emptiness guard, and the comment claims otherwise. recordCounts.isEmpty() at line 64 runs on the CALLER's map; Map.copyOf is at line 74; the comment above it says 'Copy FIRST, then validate the copy: validating the caller's own map leaves a window in which it can change between check and copy' -- which is true of the loop below it and false of the check above it. The backlog row repeats the claim as 'recordCounts copied FIRST then validated'. Corollary: after Map.copyOf, which itself rejects null keys and null values with NPE, the Objects.requireNonNull(e.getKey()) at line 76 and the e.getValue() == null branch at line 77 are unreachable -- the fix turned two live guards into dead code, and no test can cover them, so deleting either survives mutation.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller races: passes a one-entry map, another thread clears it between the isEmpty() check and Map.copyOf. The request is constructed with an empty recordCounts, the guard the task explicitly placed at the seam ('refused at the seam rather than layers down in CommitDelta') is bypassed, and the caller learns at CommitDelta's constructor instead -- 'a delta with no runs commits nothing' -- which is the exact layering the row says this guard prevents. (Racing a plain HashMap through Map.copyOf is undefined regardless; the finding is that the comment and the backlog row assert a property the code does not have.)

findings.summary: F5's @return warning is correct that an M4.7 delta may carry other callers' runs, but the remedy it prescribes is not achievable with the current format and quietly constrains a decision M4.7 owns. It tells a caller to 'select by the RunKeys it asked for'. CommitDelta carries no pod attribution and RunCommit is (RunKey, recordCount, firstOffset) with no podId, so when two pods commit the SAME RunKey inside one commitBatchInterval -- M4.7's row: 'one delta carries every stream AND every contributing pod flush in its window' -- selection by RunKey cannot separate them. Either the runs are merged (one RunCommit whose offset range spans both pods' records) or the list holds two entries with the same key and no way to tell them apart.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.7 lands with merged per-stream runs. A caller follows this javadoc, selects the single RunCommit for its RunKey, and acks firstOffset..lastOffset to its producer -- a range that includes another pod's records. It acks records it never wrote, and the offsets it reports for its own records are wrong. The safer statement is the bound only ('a returned delta may carry runs this caller did not submit; how a caller identifies its own is settled by M4.7'), leaving the mechanism to the task that owns it -- the same lesson M4.0's round 3 recorded about specifying a mechanism a spec need not contain.

findings.summary: close() is the one member of the seam with no stated contract, on an interface whose task is 'the interface's stated contract'. Nothing says whether close is idempotent, whether commit after close throws, or -- once M4.7 batches -- whether close flushes or discards a pending batch. FakeSequencer's close() is an empty method, so the fake remains fully functional after close, and FakeSequencer's javadoc claims 'IT HONOURS THE SAME CONTRACT THE INTERFACE STATES' while the interface states nothing here to honour.
findings.failure_scenario: Another module's test uses the fixture inside try-with-resources, then commits again from a cached reference after the block. Against FakeSequencer it passes; against the real M4.2+ implementation -- which holds a lease and, from M4.7, a batching executor -- it throws or hangs. The divergence surfaces only when the fake is swapped out, which is the exact failure the fake's own javadoc says a fake that quietly differs causes.

findings.summary: Carried forward from round 1 and, on judgement, correctly left unfixed here. security.md rule 5 ('anything sized by client input has a bound -- frame lengths, batch counts, key lengths, queue depths') does not bite yet: every caller in M4 is in-process, the record's javadoc says 'from M5, a network' rather than 'today, a network', and the bound that matters for an untrusted peer is a frame length in the transport's framing, which is M5's and does not exist. Fixing it here would mean inventing a maxPodIdBytes / maxSegmentKeyBytes / maxRuns triple with no measurement behind any of them, in a commit whose task enumerates its validation set and does not include them. Noting only that nothing in the tree currently records the obligation: backlog.md holds the current milestone only, so there is no M5 row to carry it, and roadmap.md's M5 row names commit forwarding without naming the bound.
findings.failure_scenario: M5's remote Sequencer deserialises a CommitRequest from a peer without a length or cardinality bound; a malformed or hostile peer sends a 100 MB segmentKey or a recordCounts map with ten million entries and the leaseholder allocates it. Recorded so the bound is written when the transport is, not discovered then.

Round-1 test major: FakeSequencer and CommitRequest are now adequately constrained from the production side. oneCommitCarryingManyStreams... pins size 3, the sorted order, per-run recordCounts (3,5,2 -- not the first one's) and per-stream zero offsets, so .limit(1), a hardcoded count and deleting .sorted() all die. everyStreamInAMultiRunCommitAdvances... kills advancing every stream by one shared amount. nextOffsetReports... kills 'return 0L'. podIdAndFlushSeqSurviveConstruction kills pinning either field to a constant in the compact constructor, which is a real hazard here because the constructor does reassign recordCounts. theCopiedRecordCountsAreImmutable... distinguishes Map.copyOf from new HashMap<>(). Sort order verified sound: RunKey.compareTo is (indexId, partitionId) and both UUIDs in the test have msb 0 with lsb 0xaa < 0xbb, so containsExactly(a,b,c) is the true sorted order and not an accident of insertion.

No production behaviour changed in a way that needs re-checking: FakeSequencer.commit is unchanged in shape from what round 1 saw and matches CommitLog.java:122-141 -- same Map.Entry.comparingByKey() sort, same per-key nextOffset accumulation, same nextSequence++.

cost_review: No object-store request is added, moved or multiplied. Sequencer.commit is one delta per segment commit, which is the per-segment rate the architecture permits; M4.7 will reduce it further by batching. FakeSequencer is pure in-memory. No get/put/list/stat appears in this diff at all, no LIST is introduced, and no idle path issues a request. The @return note about M4.7 is cost-positive in direction. Non-negotiable 6 is not threatened by this change.
scope_and_pre_emption: No decision the spec deferred is pre-empted. There is no lease type, no lease field, no epoch, no checkpoint pointer and no discovery mechanism anywhere in the diff -- M4.3's warning about pre-adopting a checkpoint-pointer field and M4.8's mandated ADR are both untouched. Sequencer's javadoc only NAMES the lease as context ('the node holding the lease commits directly') without defining or exposing it. M4.10 is named as a debt, not implemented. Nothing widens scope beyond the task's four artifacts plus the backlog row. The backlog row is honest about both majors and the weak-test episode, including the three tests that initially passed against the skeleton and the false premise on which a field-preservation test had been deleted; its 432/17 numbers are accurate.
seam_readiness: M4.2 can build against this without inventing a decision, with two gaps: close()'s semantics (F11) and, if F7 is not corrected, whether it must implement duplicate suppression now. CommitRequest maps cleanly onto CommitLog.commit(String, Map<RunKey,Integer>) with podId/flushSeq carried and unused, which is exactly what the task intends.
